> 民不畏死，奈何以死懼之？

Chapter 73 said: the net is open and loses nothing. Chapter 74 asks a narrower question — who is allowed to close it.

## 司 is 后 turned around

司: 臣司事于外者，从反后.

后 is the ruler. 司 is 后 written reversed.

Xu Shen's gloss is devastating in its economy: turn the ruler around, and you get the officer — the one who handles affairs outside.

So the title 司殺者 excludes the man in the hall by its own structure. It does not mean "the one seated above who holds life and death." It means "the one sent outside to act according to the rule."

And a person who wants to 代 him must first reverse himself — and the reversed man is no longer the ruler.

## 代 is to take a shift

代: 更也 — to change over, to swap shifts.

So 代大匠斫 is not "usurping power." It is taking someone else's shift.

And the one taking the shift does not have the axe's skill in his hands.

## 斫 and the wound

斫 is to chop. 代大匠斫者，希有不傷其手矣 — whoever chops in the master carpenter's place rarely fails to cut his own hand.

The claim is not moral. It is the plainest possible observation about borrowed tools: the skill is in the hand that was trained, not in the tool that was handed over.

## 奇 is the unpaired one

奇: 異也，一曰不耦. 耦 is two people ploughing side by side; 不耦 is the one out of the pairing.

So 為奇者 is not "a bad person." It is the one not in the line.

Wang Bi's gloss is the most accurate available: 詭異亂群 — the strange that disorders the group.

Which relocates the whole chapter. The thing being punished is not wickedness; it is being out of formation. And the chapter's objection is that killing the unpaired is itself the act of a man who has stepped out of formation to do it.

## 民不畏死

If the people no longer fear death, what is the use of threatening them with it?

The question is not rhetorical compassion. It is an observation about a threshold: fear of death is a lever only while it is in place, and its removal is not caused by the threat — it is caused by conditions in which death has stopped being the worst option.

Chapter 75 will name those conditions.

## Why this follows 73

73: the net is open; heaven loses nothing.
74: and the one who tries to close it by hand is taking a shift he was not trained for.

The chapter is about the boundary of delegated force — and its argument is technical rather than sentimental: the hand gets cut.

## A test

Take any power you hold over someone — a rule you can enforce, a consequence you can impose. Ask whether you are 司 (acting under a rule that also binds you) or 后 (acting as the source of the rule). The cut hand belongs to the second.
